title: OrbitArk - Redwood partner integration sync
summary: Introductory partner discovery between Redwood and OrbitArk to assess integration fit: OrbitArk is a SaaS integrator/reseller targeting mid-market fintechs and evaluating GPU-accelerated inference on private and hybrid architectures. Key topics: deployment modes (hosted vs private), VPC and KMS requirements, latency/cost tradeoffs, pilot scope and timeline. Agreed next steps include a short benchmarking plan, sharing security docs, and scheduling an SE-led proof-of-concept planning session.
topics: partner business model and target customers
security & compliance: SOC2, KMS, audit logs
performance: latency targets, batching, KV cache
commercial: pilot sizing, pricing model, go-to-market
transcript:
Header: Date: 2025-08-14 | Start: 16:00 PDT | Duration: 56m
Attendees: Maya Chen, Rafael Ortiz - Redwood; Elena Park, Samir Qureshi, Lina Gomez - OrbitArk

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, welcome. quick intros from our side, I'm Maya, I'm an AE at Redwood. Rafael is our SE, he'll take the deeper infra bits.
[00:12] Elena: Hi Maya, hi Rafa, I'm Elena, Director of Partnerships at OrbitArk. We coordinate channel relationships, we work with integrators and banks, etc.
[00:20] Samir: Samir here, lead infra at OrbitArk. We run a multi-tenant SaaS for payments analytics and need GPU-backed inference for some of our newer features.
[00:30] Lina: Lina, solutions architect, I'll be hands-on with integration.
[00:35] Rafael: Great to meet you all. Quick agenda: high level business fit, infra constraints, security/compliance, performance targets, then next steps. Sound good?
[00:42] Elena: Yup.

[02:05] Maya: Can you tell us a bit about your customers and what success looks like for a partner integration? who would own the integration and sales motion?
[02:18] Elena: Sure. OrbitArk resells to mid-market fintechs and some small banks, usually 10-300 headcount. They care about data residency and auditability. Success is easy onboarding and predictable unit costs so their PMs can ship features. We'll likely own initial customer integration and co-sell with you.
[02:40] Maya: Got it. And timeline for pilots and revenue motion?
[02:46] Elena: We're aiming to run 2 pilots before end of Q4, pilots start in October ideally. If pilots go well, we want a partner pricing structure and a reference case by Q1.

[05:12] Samir: On infra: our platform is Kubernetes-based, runs in customer VPCs for some players, and we manage some customers in our own cloud tenancy. We need to understand options for Redwood Dedicated vs Private, and if there's an on-prem or air-gapped route. Also curious about GPU options and whether Redwood supports mixed instance types.
[05:40] Rafael: We support three primary modes: hosted API (fastest to ship), Dedicated reserved pools for predictable throughput, and Private deployments for VPC/on-prem where you manage network. Mixed GPU fleets are possible; runtime can route models based on capacity. Note, we sometimes see minor variance in kernel perf across different cards, but we tune profiles per fleet.
[06:05] Lina: When you say Private, does that mean the control plane still runs in Redwood and data plane in VPC, or can control plane be customer-managed?
[06:14] Rafael: Both options exist. We have a private control plane option for enterprise customers where the control plane is in their VPC and they can opt into an air-gapped package. For true air-gapped, there is an on-prem bundle. We'll share the architecture doc.

[09:00] Elena: Security checklist questions: SOC2 type II, ISO, SSO/SAML, RBAC, KMS integration for keys, and audit logs retention. Our customers sometimes require HSM-backed keys.
[09:20] Maya: We are SOC2, have SAML and SCIM support (SSO + user provisioning), RBAC, KMS integrations (we support both cloud KMS and customer-managed HSM options). Audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM. We'll send the security pack and our SOC2 report.
[09:45] Samir: Good. On encryption: do you support customer-managed keys for model artifacts and prompts, and what about tokenization/pseudonymization for PII?
[10:02] Rafael: You can use customer KMS to encrypt at-rest artifacts. For PII we recommend client-side tokenization/obfuscation before sending prompts, and we can help design a flow. We also support configurable retention policies to avoid storing prompts beyond X days.

[12:30] Lina: Performance: our target latency for short-form generation is sub-200ms p50 and p95 under 500ms for small bursts, for some customers p95 under 350ms. Are those achievable on Dedicated or Hosted?
[12:50] Rafael: Sub-200ms p50 is feasible for smaller models on high-performance instances with warm KV cache and small batching. p95 depends on burst patterns; Dedicated with reserved warm pools gives best predictability. We also do prefix/KV caching to keep latencies tight. If you need strict p95 SLAs, Dedicated or co-located Private is safer.
[13:25] Samir: What's the overhead of our own ingress layer + VPC peering? we worry about network egress latency adding variability.
[13:34] Rafael: Network adds some variability, but we can co-locate edge proxies or leverage direct connect / private links to cut hops. We'll propose network topology options in the follow-up doc.

[17:10] Elena: Commercial: do you have partner pricing or reseller tiers? Also curious about meter granularity: per-token, per-embedding, or bundled pilot rates?
[17:24] Maya: For pilots we usually offer a time-boxed discounted pilot SKU with included tokens and test quota. Production pricing is usage-based (tokens / embeddings) and for Dedicated there's reserved capacity contracts. We have partner margins for resellers; we'll share a partner program deck.

[20:45] Lina: Tech question: model lifecycle and rollouts — can OrbitArk pin specific model versions for a customer and do canary/A-B style rollouts?
[20:58] Rafael: Yes, you can pin versions per route/customer. The Console supports canary and A/B, rollbacks, and automatic fallback policies to cheaper model variants if capacity is constrained. There can be small differences in quantized variants; we'll walk through eval tradeoffs in a later session.

[24:00] Samir: Benchmarks: we need guidance for how to run a reproducible benchmark in our environment. ideally a script we can run inside our test cluster hitting both Dedicated and Private options.
[24:12] Rafael: We'll provide a benchmarking harness — a loadgen script, sample prompt sets, and instructions for measuring p50/p95, throughput, and tokens/sec. We'll also include suggested batch sizes and model/quantization recommendations per workload.

[28:40] Elena: Competitors question: some prospects ask about AWS Bedrock, GCP Vertex, and other inference vendors. how do you position Redwood vs those?
[28:55] Maya: We position based on production economics and unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private. Unlike some managed vendor endpoints, Redwood's offering includes strong observability, cost controls (batching/caching suggestions), and explicit operational playbooks for rollouts. We typically partner with cloud providers rather than replace them — customers can deploy Private or Dedicated on cloud infra of choice.

[33:10] Lina: Integration points: do you expose SDKs for Java/Node/Python and webhooks for inference events?
[33:22] Rafael: Yes — REST + SDKs for Python/Node/Java, streaming responses, and webhook/event hooks for lifecycle events. We'll share sample SDK snippets and a quickstart repo link.

[36:50] Maya: Quick note from product: Redwood Optimize recommendations can auto-suggest batching/quantization for workloads to hit cost targets without big latency regressions. that might be useful for your customers who want predictable unit economics.
[37:10] Elena: That sounds valuable, especially for customers watching cost per transaction.

[40:00] Samir: What about regulatory/data residency: some customers require EU-only hosting or even country-specific. can we pin deployments to regions?
[40:12] Rafael: Yes, we support region pinning for deployments and data residency. For stricter cases we recommend Private deployments in the region or on-prem bundles. We'll document options for EU-only footprints.

[44:05] Lina: A few gotchas we've seen: vendor drivers mismatch on custom kernels, and sometimes quantization introduces hallucination differences. do you have guardrails or evaluation tooling?
[44:20] Rafael: We have evaluation harnesses and quality monitoring with regression alerts tied to prompt sets. For quantization, we produce recommendations and quality deltas, and can keep a non-quantized fallback for critical routes.

[48:00] Elena: Ok, let's recap and next steps.
[48:10] Maya: Recap: 1) Redwood to share security pack + SOC2; 2) Redwood to share architecture doc for Private control plane and network topology options; 3) Rafael to share benchmarking harness and quickstart repo; 4) OrbitArk to pick two pilot customers and send pilot requirements by 2025-09-05; 5) schedule SE-led pilot planning session (60m) in early September.
[48:45] Samir: We can target pilot candidate list by Sept 5.
[49:00] Lina: We'll need a call to map integration points with our provisioning flow; I'll own that.
[49:10] Maya: Great. Any final questions?
[49:20] Elena: Not for now. Thanks everyone.
[55:30] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up in the notes with links. bye.
